Can You Get Dental Implants If You Take ADHD Medication?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you take medication for ADHD and are considering dental implants, you may have found yourself wondering whether your prescription could affect your eligibility for treatment — or how it might influence the healing process. This is a question many adults in London and across the UK are asking, particularly as ADHD diagnoses in adults have become more widely recognised in recent years.

It is entirely understandable to search for answers online before discussing treatment options with your dental team. Dental implants represent a significant clinical procedure, and if you are managing a condition such as ADHD, it is natural to want to understand all the relevant factors in advance.

Dental implants and ADHD medication sit at an interesting crossroads of medical and dental considerations. Certain ADHD medications — particularly stimulant-based options such as methylphenidate or amphetamine salts — can influence oral health in ways that may be relevant to implant planning. This article explains the key factors involved, what your dental team will assess, and why an open conversation about your medical history is so important.

In many cases, yes — dental implants may still be a suitable option for patients taking ADHD medication. However, suitability depends on individual clinical assessment. Certain ADHD medications can cause dry mouth and teeth grinding, which may affect oral health and implant planning. A thorough dental evaluation is always required before any treatment decisions are made.

What Is ADHD and How Is It Typically Managed?

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects concentration, impulse control, and behaviour. It is increasingly diagnosed in adults as well as children, and treatment commonly involves a combination of behavioural strategies and prescribed medication.

The two main classes of ADHD medication are:

  • Stimulant medications — such as methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) and amphetamine-based drugs (Adderall, Vyvanse). These are the most commonly prescribed and work by increasing dopamine and noradrenaline activity in the brain.
  • Non-stimulant medications — such as atomoxetine (Strattera) and guanfacine, which are sometimes used when stimulants are not suitable or well tolerated.

Both categories can have side effects that are relevant to dental health. Understanding these effects is an important part of dental implant planning when a patient is taking ADHD medication. Your dental team will want to understand your full medical history, including the specific medication you take, the dose, and how long you have been on it, before making any clinical recommendations.

How ADHD Medication Can Affect Oral Health

This is perhaps the most important area to understand before exploring dental implants. ADHD medication — particularly stimulant-based treatments — can have several effects on the mouth that may have a bearing on implant suitability and long-term success.

Dry Mouth (Xerostomia)

Stimulant medications are well-documented to reduce saliva production, leading to a condition known as dry mouth or xerostomia. Saliva plays a critical role in protecting the teeth and gums — it neutralises acids, washes away food debris, and contains antimicrobial properties. When saliva flow is reduced, the risk of tooth decay, gum disease, and oral infections increases. All of these factors are clinically relevant when planning dental implant treatment, as a healthy oral environment is essential for implant success.

Bruxism (Teeth Grinding)

Stimulant medications are also associated with bruxism — the involuntary grinding or clenching of teeth. Bruxism can cause significant wear on natural teeth and, in patients with existing dental implants, may place excessive stress on the implant crown and surrounding bone. For those considering implant treatment, managing bruxism before and after the procedure is often part of a comprehensive treatment plan.

Increased Sugar Cravings

Some patients taking ADHD medication report cravings for sugary foods and drinks, partly as a response to the appetite suppression stimulants can cause. Frequent sugar consumption increases the risk of tooth decay and gum disease — conditions that can compromise both natural teeth and dental implant sites.

The Clinical Science: Why Oral Health Matters for Dental Implants

To understand why your dental team pays close attention to oral health conditions before placing implants, it helps to understand how dental implants work at a biological level.

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone, where it serves as an artificial tooth root. Over a period of weeks to months, the implant undergoes a process called osseointegration — where the surrounding bone tissue bonds directly to the surface of the titanium. This bond is what gives the implant its strength and stability.

For osseointegration to be successful, the implant site must be free from infection, and the surrounding bone must be in good condition. This means that any factors affecting bone health, gum health, or the body's ability to heal — including the oral health side effects of certain medications — are clinically important.

Dry mouth caused by ADHD medication, for example, creates an environment more prone to bacterial growth and infection. Untreated gum disease (periodontitis) is a significant risk factor for implant failure. Similarly, unmanaged bruxism can apply excessive mechanical force on a healing implant, potentially disrupting the osseointegration process.

This does not mean that patients taking ADHD medication cannot have dental implants — rather, it means these factors need to be carefully assessed and, where necessary, managed before treatment begins. To learn more about how dental implants work and what the procedure involves, visit the dental implants treatment page.

If your prescription profile includes wakefulness medication or overlapping sleep-related treatment, this companion guide on dental implants and narcolepsy medication may also be relevant.

What Your Dental Team Will Assess Before Recommending Implants

A thorough pre-treatment assessment is a fundamental part of responsible dental implant planning. For patients taking ADHD medication, this assessment is likely to include several specific considerations:

Medical History Review

Your dental team will ask for a complete and up-to-date medical history, including the name and dosage of your ADHD medication, any other prescribed drugs, and details of any other health conditions. If you are working with a psychiatrist or GP to manage your ADHD, your dental team may wish to liaise with them to ensure that any planned treatment is coordinated appropriately.

Oral Health Examination

Before implant treatment is considered, your dentist will carry out a thorough assessment of your gum health, bone levels, and the condition of your remaining teeth. Any active gum disease, infection, or untreated decay will typically need to be addressed before implant placement can be planned.

Bone Density Assessment

Dental implants require sufficient bone volume and density for successful placement. X-rays and, where appropriate, CBCT (cone beam computed tomography) scanning may be used to evaluate the available bone structure at the proposed implant site.

Assessment of Bruxism

If there is evidence of teeth grinding — such as worn tooth surfaces or jaw discomfort — your dental team may recommend that this is managed before or alongside implant treatment. A custom-made night guard is a common and effective approach.

Managing Dry Mouth to Support Implant Health

If your ADHD medication is causing dry mouth, there are practical steps you and your dental team can work on together to protect your oral health and support long-term implant success.

Staying well hydrated is one of the simplest and most effective strategies. Drinking water regularly throughout the day — including plain water between meals — helps compensate for reduced saliva production.

Alcohol-free mouthwashes and saliva substitutes are available over the counter and may help maintain moisture levels in the mouth. Your dental team can recommend specific products suited to your needs.

Fluoride-based products — including high-fluoride toothpaste if prescribed — can help protect teeth from the increased decay risk associated with dry mouth.

Regular dental check-ups are particularly important for patients with dry mouth. More frequent hygiene appointments may be recommended to monitor gum health and catch early signs of decay or gum disease around the implant site. Learn more about how structured dental implant maintenance care supports long-term oral health.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Particularly Important

Whilst this article provides general educational information, there are certain situations where seeking a dental assessment sooner rather than later is advisable — particularly if you are considering dental implants and take ADHD medication.

You may wish to arrange a dental consultation if you notice any of the following:

  • Persistent dry mouth that is affecting your comfort or eating, or that you feel is worsening over time
  • Signs of gum disease, such as bleeding gums when brushing, swollen or red gum tissue, or gum recession around existing teeth
  • Jaw pain, facial discomfort, or worn teeth, which may indicate bruxism
  • Tooth loss or significant tooth damage, which is prompting you to explore tooth replacement options such as implants
  • Sensitivity or pain around existing teeth or any previous dental restorations

None of these symptoms necessarily mean that implant treatment is unsuitable — but they do indicate that a clinical assessment would be valuable. Early evaluation allows your dental team to address any underlying issues and put together a treatment plan that accounts for your individual medical and dental circumstances.

If you are ready to proceed, reviewing the implant consultation and booking options can help you plan your next step.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice for Patients Taking ADHD Medication

Whether or not dental implants are part of your future treatment plan, maintaining good oral health whilst taking ADHD medication is important. Here are some practical steps to support your dental wellbeing:

  • Brush twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste, ideally after morning medication when appetite suppression may have reduced your food intake
  • Clean between teeth daily using interdental brushes or floss to remove plaque from areas your toothbrush cannot reach
  • Choose water over sugary drinks, particularly when managing appetite suppression side effects that may lead to grazing on snacks throughout the day
  • Chew sugar-free gum to help stimulate saliva production if dry mouth is a concern — look for products containing xylitol, which has additional protective properties
  • Avoid alcohol-containing mouthwashes, which can worsen dry mouth
  • Attend regular dental check-ups — your dentist can recommend the appropriate frequency based on your individual risk profile
  • Inform your dentist about any changes to your medication, including dose adjustments or switching between medications, as this may affect your oral health management plan

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants and ADHD medication are not automatically incompatible — suitability depends on individual clinical assessment
  • Stimulant ADHD medications can cause dry mouth and bruxism, both of which are relevant to implant planning and long-term success
  • Maintaining a healthy oral environment before and after implant treatment is essential for osseointegration and implant longevity
  • A thorough pre-treatment dental assessment will evaluate your gum health, bone levels, and any medication-related oral health factors
  • Open communication with your dental team about your medical history and ADHD medication is essential for safe and effective treatment planning
  • Preventative measures — including hydration, fluoride use, and regular hygiene appointments — can help mitigate the oral health effects of ADHD medication

Frequently Asked Questions

Will I need to stop taking my ADHD medication before dental implant surgery?

In most cases, patients are advised to continue their prescribed ADHD medication as normal before dental procedures, unless specifically directed otherwise by their prescribing doctor. Stopping ADHD medication suddenly is generally not recommended without medical guidance. Your dental team will discuss your medication with you and, if necessary, liaise with your GP or psychiatrist to ensure your care is coordinated safely. Never adjust or discontinue prescribed medication without seeking medical advice first.

Can dry mouth caused by ADHD medication cause a dental implant to fail?

Dry mouth itself does not directly cause implant failure, but it creates conditions in the mouth that increase the risk of gum disease and infection — both of which are risk factors for implant complications. With appropriate preventative management, including more frequent hygiene appointments and good home care, many patients with dry mouth successfully maintain dental implants long term. Your dental team will advise you on a personalised care plan.

How does teeth grinding (bruxism) affect dental implants?

Bruxism places excessive mechanical pressure on teeth, restorations, and implants. For dental implants, this force — if unmanaged — can potentially affect the osseointegration process or cause damage to the implant crown over time. A custom-fitted night guard is often recommended for patients with bruxism who have dental implants. Your dentist will assess the presence and severity of bruxism as part of your implant treatment planning.

Are non-stimulant ADHD medications less likely to cause dental problems?

Non-stimulant medications such as atomoxetine may carry a lower risk of dry mouth and bruxism compared to stimulant medications, though individual responses vary. All medications can have side effects, and your dental team will assess your oral health regardless of the specific medication you take. It is always worth mentioning all prescribed medications — stimulant or otherwise — at your dental appointments.

How long does the dental implant process take for someone taking ADHD medication?

The overall implant treatment timeline is similar for most patients and typically spans several months, primarily due to the time required for osseointegration. For patients whose ADHD medication has contributed to gum disease or significant bone loss, additional preparatory treatment may be needed before implant placement, which can extend the overall timeline. Your dental team will provide a realistic treatment plan based on your individual clinical assessment.

Is there anything I should tell my dentist before starting implant treatment?

Yes — it is important to provide your dental team with a complete and accurate medical history, including all prescribed medications, supplements, and any other health conditions. For patients taking ADHD medication, relevant information includes the specific medication name, dosage, and duration of use. If you have previously experienced bruxism, dry mouth, or significant dental issues, share this history too. This information helps your dental team plan treatment safely and effectively for your individual circumstances.

Conclusion

Taking ADHD medication does not automatically prevent you from being a candidate for dental implants, but it does introduce factors that your dental team needs to carefully consider during the planning process. The most common concerns — dry mouth, bruxism, and the increased risk of gum disease — are manageable with the right approach, and many patients taking ADHD medication go on to have successful implant treatment.

What matters most is open, honest communication with your dental team about your medical history and current medication. A thorough clinical assessment will determine whether implants are appropriate for you and identify any steps needed to optimise your oral health before treatment begins.

Maintaining excellent oral hygiene habits, attending regular check-ups, and working with both your dental and medical teams as partners in your care will give you a strong foundation for your care — whether you proceed with dental implants or explore treatment choices for missing teeth suited to your circumstances.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional. Treatment outcomes and timelines vary between individuals.
